primary_meaning: In Christian teaching, fig leaves most commonly symbolize humanity's inadequate self-effort to cover sin and shame — human-made righteousness or self-justification that cannot truly atone. The image comes from Adam and Eve sewing fig leaves together after the Fall, a covering routinely contrasted in sermons and commentaries with the garments of skin God later provides (often read as pointing to divinely provided atonement through sacrifice, and typologically toward Christ). Closely bound up with this is the meaning of shame and the newly awakened consciousness of sin.
primary_basis: Genesis 3:7 (Adam and Eve sew fig leaves to cover their nakedness)
Genesis 3:21 (God clothes them with garments of skin, the standard contrast text)
Genesis 2:25 (prior state of nakedness without shame, establishing the shame motif)
Isaiah 64:6 (righteous deeds as filthy rags — commonly paired to support the 'self-righteousness' reading)

alternatives.meaning: Hypocrisy or fruitless outward show: leaves without fruit, drawn from Jesus cursing the fig tree that had leaves but no figs — profession of religion without genuine fruit. Often extended to Israel's spiritual barrenness or, more broadly, to empty religiosity.
basis: Luke 13:6-9 (parable of the barren fig tree)

alternatives.meaning: Shame, guilt, and the loss of innocence per se — fig leaves simply as the emblem of fallen humanity's new awareness of exposure before God, without the further 'works-righteousness' polemic.
The fig tree/fig leaves as a symbol of national Israel (especially in prophetic and dispensational interpretation), where the budding fig tree signals Israel's restoration or eschatological timing.
A tradition (found in some rabbinic and patristic speculation) that the fig was the actual tree of knowledge, making the fig leaves an ironic covering taken from the very tree of transgression.
basis: Genesis 3:6-7 (inference from the immediate availability of fig leaves)
Rabbinic sources such as Genesis Rabbah; echoed by some church fathers

alternatives.meaning: An origin account of clothing and modesty, read historically or morally rather than symbolically — fig leaves as the first garments, teaching modesty after the Fall.

notes: There is a broadly recognizable consensus in popular and homiletical Christian usage: 'fig leaves' functions almost proverbially for inadequate human attempts to cover sin (self-righteousness), grounded in the Genesis 3:7 vs. 3:21 contrast. The hypocrisy/fruitlessness reading from the Gospel fig-tree episodes is also widespread but attaches more to the fig tree than to the leaves specifically; the two motifs are frequently blended in preaching (leaves = appearance, fruit = reality). Academic biblical scholarship is more restrained, often treating Genesis 3:7 as an etiology of shame and clothing rather than a doctrine of works-righteousness, so the strength of the 'self-effort' consensus is higher in devotional/evangelical teaching than in critical scholarship.
